statement: A cache is a data-storage component that can be read faster or more cheaply than the original source, holding a temporary copy so repeated access to the same data is served faster and with fewer resources.

Caching is applied at many layers: common cache types include HTTP application caches, HTTP network (intermediate/CDN) caches, browser caches, service caches, API-response caches, database caches, CPU instruction caches, memory caches, and disk caches.
A cache adds value only when the operation to calculate or retrieve the data is slow or resource-intensive in the first place.
condition: deciding whether caching will add value

statement: A cache adds value only if it can store and return the result faster and with fewer resources than the original source would.
condition: deciding whether caching will add value

statement: Caching is easier and more reliable when data does not change between requests; dynamically changing data can be cached only in certain circumstances.
exception: data that changes between requests is harder to cache and cacheable only in limited circumstances

statement: A cacheable operation should have no side effects beyond resource consumption: it should not store data, change other systems, or control other software or hardware.
exception: a side-effecting operation may be cached only if its side-effect actions are handled correctly

statement: A cache is only worthwhile when the same data is needed more than once; the more often a result is reused, the more effective the cache is.
condition: deciding whether caching will add value

statement: Cache effectiveness depends on the statistical distribution of data access: a normal (bell-curve) access distribution makes caching more likely to be effective than a flat distribution.
exception: advanced caching strategies can be more effective for other access distributions

statement: Caches fall into two fundamental usage patterns — static (read-only) and dynamic (read/write) — distinguished by how the cache is updated when the underlying data store changes.
In a dynamic (read/write) cache the application writes changes directly into the cache, so when a store value changes the cached value is overwritten in place.

In a static (read-only) cache the cached entry is immutable to the application; updates are written to the underlying store and the stale entry is removed, so the next read misses and reloads the new value from the store.

Caching reduces latency, and because latency is a primary driver of user-perceived outages, avoiding time-intensive recomputation through cache hits materially improves application performance over time.
Caching improves scalability by reducing redundant resource consumption, letting an application operate at higher scale before its resources become saturated.
Caching optimizes resource use by avoiding expensive recomputation of costly operations, which lowers required compute/memory and can improve throughput.
Caching improves availability: when a cached result is present it can be returned even if the underlying resources are busy, offline, or otherwise unavailable.
Caching is not universally beneficial: in many situations it adds no value, and in some cases it actively degrades performance.

When deciding whether and how to cache, evaluate three specific risks: that caching suppresses desired side effects of the operation, that cached data becomes inconsistent, and that cache performance is poor.
A service has a side effect if it modifies state — virtual or physical — outside its own local environment, such as writing to a database or actuating hardware.
Do not cache a side-effecting service without explicitly handling its side effects: improperly caching operations with side effects is a common cause of software failures and outages.
condition: the operation being cached has side effects

statement: A cache is said to be inconsistent when the value it holds does not match the current value in the backing data store.
Maintaining cache consistency can be difficult and cached results easily fall out of sync with the backing store, depending on the caching pattern chosen.
condition: depends on the caching pattern in use

statement: In a cache-aside pattern, a cache is only effective when the resources needed to check and fill the cache are significantly smaller than the resources needed to perform the backing operation.

A cache is only effective when hits (the cache holds the correct, current response) significantly outnumber misses; if the correct response is usually absent, the overhead of checking the cache can make performance worse.
If manipulating the cache costs more than the backing operation, or if cache hits are rare, the cache degrades performance and should not be deployed in production.

A cache is a temporary store placed in front of the system of record that is faster either because its medium is physically faster (e.g., RAM versus disk) or because it sits physically/logically nearer the data consumer (e.g., an edge location or local client).

The standard cache data-flow is: check the cache first; on a hit read directly from the cache; on a miss fetch from the underlying store and then populate the cache so future reads are served from it.
Caching strategies can be divided by how data flows through the cache into inline caches and cache-aside caches.

An inline cache sits in front of the data store so the store is accessed through the cache; it covers read-through, write-through, and read/write-through variants, and the cache itself is responsible for maintaining consistency.

In a cache-aside pattern the cache is accessed independently of the data store with no direct cache-to-store connection; the application handles all operations to both, and the application is responsible for cache consistency.
The cache-aside read flow is: the application checks the cache; on a miss it reads the value from the data store directly, then writes it into the cache; subsequent reads are served from the cache.
Cache consistency is the measure of whether the value stored in the cache equals the source value in the underlying data store, and maintaining it is essential to using a cache successfully.
Cache inconsistency typically arises when the underlying data changes and the cache is not updated with the new value in a timely manner.
Cache invalidation — removing a value from the cache once it is determined to be out of date — is the most basic technique for maintaining cache consistency.

Invalidate-on-write maintains consistency in a cache-aside pattern: write the new value to the data store and remove the key from the cache, so the next read misses and reloads the current value from the store.

In a write-through cache the application writes the new value to the cache and the cache synchronously updates the data store, so both hold the new value and the cache remains consistent; the cache owns consistency.
The downside of a write-through cache is that each write is relatively slow because it must update both the cache and the slower backing data store (two writes, one to the slow backend).

A write-behind (write-back) cache updates only the cache and returns the write immediately, then asynchronously updates the underlying data store later in the background, making application writes fast.

Write-behind trades speed for consistency: between the cache write and the asynchronous store update the cache holds the correct value while the store is stale, so any read that bypasses the cache and hits the store directly can return the old value until the flush completes.
exception: tolerable only if the application requirements permit a temporary inconsistency window and reads do not bypass the cache

statement: A cache is typically smaller than the underlying data store and therefore holds only a subset of the data, so a key job of the cache is to determine and keep available the data that will be needed.
When a full cache must store new data, an eviction policy decides what to remove; delegating that responsibility to the application is called the All-In or no-eviction policy.
Cache eviction is the removal of older or less-frequently-used data to make room for new data; evicted data must be re-fetched from the underlying store if it is needed again later.

A least-recently-used (LRU) eviction policy evicts the entry that has not been accessed for the longest time, on the premise that data not accessed recently is less likely to be accessed in the future.
A least-frequently-used (LFU) eviction policy evicts the entry accessed the fewest times; LRU keys its decision on last-access time (recency) whereas LFU keys it on access count (frequency).
An oldest-stored (first-in-first-out) eviction policy evicts the entry that has been resident in the cache the longest; it is not common in enterprise caches.

Random eviction removes a randomly selected entry; it is easy and fast to implement but more likely to evict still-needed data, producing more later cache misses, so it is not typically used in production.
Time-to-live (TTL) eviction gives each value a lifetime after which it is removed whether or not the cache is full; in Redis TTL is set per key, not via the cache-eviction policy.

Session management is a common TTL use case: a session object's TTL represents the idle-logout interval and is refreshed on every user interaction, so if the user stops interacting the session is evicted and the user is logged out.

A persistent (no-eviction) cache never evicts data; once full it rejects new data until space is freed, so the simpler no-algorithm approach is suitable only when the cache is large enough to hold the entire dataset.
condition: the cache can hold all of the underlying data

statement: Cache thrashing occurs when an evicted value is re-requested soon after and re-fetched, displacing other values in a back-and-forth that reduces cache efficiency; it typically happens when the cache is full and using an eviction policy ill-suited to the use case, and can often be reduced by changing the eviction algorithm or increasing the cache size.

There is no universally correct eviction strategy; the right choice depends on the application's needs and access patterns, LRU or LFU is usually the best choice, and selecting between them generally requires analyzing data access patterns or using trial and error.

A cold cache is empty at startup so all requests miss and performance is poor, while a warm cache has been populated so hits rise and performance improves over time; seeding a cache initially is called cache warming/warmup and adding data continuously over time is called pre-fetching.
To avoid poor performance from a cold start, static-data caches are often seeded (warmed) before serving traffic, unlike session caches which commonly start empty.

Redis is an in-memory (RAM) store, which makes it fast, and is commonly used as a cache front end for a slower but more permanent data store such as an SQL database; it can also persist its data, for example to automatically warm the cache during recovery.
As a cache, open-source Redis is typically used in a cache-aside strategy, so the logic to manage the cache lives in the application using it.

By default a full Redis database rejects further writes (implementing a no-eviction policy); setting maxmemory-policy to allkeys-lru, allkeys-lfu, or allkeys-random enables eviction across all keys, while the volatile-* variants restrict eviction to keys that have an expiration set.

Redis LRU and LFU eviction policies are approximations: rather than deleting the true least-recently/least-frequently-used key, Redis samples several keys and evicts the best candidate among the sample, which closely approximates the ideal while using significantly less memory.

A volatile cache exists in memory and is erased on a power outage or system restart, so its contents cannot be assumed available; systems must be designed to remain functional (possibly with reduced performance) even if the cache is wiped.

Cache persistence stores a cache's contents in persistent storage so they survive power outages and reboots; a persistent cache may be chosen for performance only when it is acceptable for the application to fail if a value is removed inappropriately.
exception: acceptable only if the application can tolerate failure when a relied-upon value is removed

statement: Volatile caches are typically implemented in RAM and persistent caches on disk/SSD, but a persistent cache can be built on volatile memory provided the cache mechanism makes redundant backups to persistent storage and rehydrates from them after a wipe.
Cache rehydration is the process of re-creating a volatile cache's contents — from either a persistent backup medium or the backing data store — before the cache comes back online after a failure.

Redis append-only-file (AOF) persistence logs every update to the cache in real time, and replaying that log on restart re-creates the cache state, turning a primarily RAM-based cache into a reliable persistent cache.

Redis AOF durability is controlled by APPENDFSYNC (no = let the OS flush when it chooses; everysec = flush once per second; always = flush after every entry); only APPENDFSYNC always guarantees that a system crash causes no data loss, while everysec and no trade durability for performance.
condition: a true no-data-loss persistent cache is required
exception: everysec or no are acceptable if the business can tolerate some cache loss on a crash

statement: BGREWRITEAOF compacts the AOF into the shortest command sequence that reproduces the current cache state; the recommended best practice is to have this run automatically rather than manually.
Redis RDB persistence creates a point-in-time snapshot file (dump.rdb) of the whole cache; SAVE creates it synchronously (blocking) and BGSAVE returns immediately and creates it in a background job.

For surviving process and system crashes only AOF with APPENDFSYNC always is reliable; RDB provides consistent point-in-time snapshots suited to historical and recovery backups but loses any changes made between snapshots on a failure, so use AOF and RDB together for both crash-tolerance and historical snapshots.

Open-source Redis requires both keys and values to be stored entirely in RAM, whereas Redis Enterprise's Redis on Flash (RoF) keeps keys in RAM but stores values across a mix of RAM and SSD by an LRU policy (hot values in RAM, colder values on SSD), enabling significantly larger and more cost-effective caches because SSD is larger and cheaper than RAM.
Using SSD via Redis on Flash does not by itself make a cache persistent, because the keys remain in RAM; AOF and/or RDB backups are still required to create a true persistent cache.

Redis can execute arbitrary functions inside the cache database (for example Python scripts via the RedisGears RG.PYEXECUTE command), enabling in-database processing and complex caching mechanisms including write-through and write-behind patterns.

The most common use of Redis in a microservices architecture is as an asynchronous communication channel — a high-speed queue (using the Redis Lists type) for passing commands, responses, and data between neighboring services.

Microservices can use Redis as a classic cache in several placements: a server-side internal cache for a service's interim data, a cache-aside distributed cache fronting a slower data store, a client-side cache of interim results to reduce backend calls, or a network-level HTTP cache between two services.

HTTP-level caching between services is managed via HTTP headers such as Cache-Control, Expires, and Last-Modified, which are typically processed by intermediaries such as reverse proxies (e.g., Nginx).

RediSearch (a Redis Enterprise module) is a secondary-index, query, and full-text search engine over Redis that lets you run SQL-like queries against indexed Hash keys with improved performance from the secondary index.
A typical cache is a key-value store; in Redis the basic value type is a String, but Redis additionally supports richer value data types beyond simple strings or numbers.

The Redis Lists type is an ordered list of strings supporting FIFO-queue semantics (e.g., LPUSH to add on the left, RPOP to remove from the right), and is most commonly used for queues and scheduling, including ordering or prioritizing data stored in a cache.

The Redis Sets type is an unordered collection of unique strings (a duplicate insert is stored only once), making it well suited to existence tests (SISMEMBER) such as detecting whether an operation was already requested from a given IP address.

The Redis Hashes type stores a set of field-value pairs under a single key, modeling a structured object (such as a user's properties) and allowing individual fields to be read and updated independently.
The RedisJSON module stores arbitrary JSON documents in a single Redis key and allows element-level get and set of individual fields within the document.

Redis supports many data types (including Sorted Sets and Streams), some of which suit traditional database use cases more than cache use cases; Redis can serve as both a cache and a primary NoSQL database, and that versatility is one of its key strengths.

Caches themselves hit performance limits at scale, of two kinds: storage limits (the space available to hold cached data) and resource limits (the cache's capacity to store and retrieve data, typically bounded by network bandwidth or CPU).

A storage limit is reached when the number of unique cached items exceeds the cache's capacity, forcing results to be discarded and turning the full cache into a bottleneck for ongoing application scaling.
A resource limit can be reached even when only one value is cached: enough repeated retrievals of the same value will eventually exhaust the network bandwidth or CPU the cache needs to serve them.
A cache is scaled by increasing its storage and/or resource limits, and there are two primary approaches: vertical scaling and horizontal scaling.

Vertical scaling (scaling up/down) increases the resources of a single cache node — typically a more powerful machine or larger cloud instance — adding RAM to ease storage limits and adding CPU and network bandwidth to ease resource limits.

Horizontal scaling (scaling out/in) adds more cache nodes to a cluster without changing the size of any individual instance, and depending on implementation can also improve cache reliability and therefore application availability.

Read replicas (in open-source Redis) improve read performance without significantly affecting write performance: auxiliary servers each hold a complete copy of the cache and serve reads, while writes go to the master, which propagates the changes to all replicas to keep them consistent.

Read replicas do not improve write performance, but they increase read throughput by spreading read load across servers and improve availability — a crashed replica's load shifts to other servers, and a replica can be promoted to master if the master fails.

Sharding raises both storage and resource limits by partitioning data across shards, each holding a portion of the cache; a shard selector (a proxy in Redis Enterprise) routes each read/write using a deterministic algorithm on the cache key, so every request for a given key goes to the one shard that holds it.

Sharding can scale cache capacity and performance roughly linearly with the number of shards (e.g., three shards nearly triple performance and storage in open-source Redis), but it is not always simple: balancing traffic across shards requires tuning, and it can lower availability because failure of a single shard instance, if not properly managed, can bring down the entire cache.
exception: Redis Clustering mitigates the tuning and availability downsides

statement: Redis Clustering simplifies sharding by using a CRC16 of the key to select one of up to ~1,000 nodes holding the data, with a re-sharding protocol for rebalancing capacity/performance and failover protocols to improve availability.

In open-source Redis, clustering is implemented client-side and requires a cluster-aware client library, whereas Redis Enterprise provides clustering server-side via a proxy protocol so any client can use the clustered cache.

Active-Active (multi-master) replication scales both read and write load: multiple nodes each hold a complete copy of the cache (so it does not raise the storage limit), a load balancer distributes requests, and a write received by one node is propagated to all others; it also improves availability because surviving nodes absorb a failed node's load.

Multi-master replication introduces write conflicts: concurrent updates to the same key can reach different masters and generate conflicting propagated updates, so a conflict-resolution algorithm is required; data lag also means nodes may hold different values for a time, and a poorly designed resolution algorithm can leave the cache inconsistent.

Open-source Redis does not natively support multi-master redundancy; Redis Enterprise Active-Active Geo-Distribution places master instances in different regions, routes each consumer to the nearest instance, and synchronizes all instances so every one holds a complete, up-to-date copy and can accept reads and writes on any key as peers.

Redis Enterprise Active-Active uses conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) to resolve write conflicts, guaranteeing strong eventual consistency and more reliable replication sync, but the application must still be written to account for data lag and write conflicts so they do not cause problems.
Which cache-scaling technique to use, if any, depends on the application's architecture and requirements and the organization's goals.
Active-Active geo-replication can continue to handle both read and write operations even when the majority of geo-replicated regions are down, and delivers local read/write latency in each region.
Maintaining cache consistency is one of the greatest challenges of operating a cache, so choosing the right caching pattern is essential.

An inconsistent cache returns a stored value that no longer matches the source; such inconsistencies can be difficult to detect and to remove, and whether they are a serious problem depends on how the application uses the data.
A cache becomes inconsistent in three main ways: the underlying data changes and the cache is not updated; there is a delay in updating cached results; or there is inconsistency across cached nodes.

In a cache-aside pattern, if the underlying value changes while the old value remains cached, future requests keep returning the stale value; consistency is restored only by updating the cached entry to the new value or removing it so the next read fetches the correct value from the store.

When the data store changes a value it notifies the cache to remove or update the entry, but that processing takes time, and any request arriving after the change but before the cache is updated returns the stale, inconsistent value.
The cache-update delay should be kept as short as possible, and whether the delay causes a problem depends entirely on the use case, which the specific application must decide.

To cache dynamically changing data, set an expire time so cached values are discarded and re-read from the store at regular intervals, which bounds how long a value can be inconsistent (e.g., a 15-minute expiry keeps a social-media like count accurate to within 15 minutes); this reduces but does not eliminate inconsistency, so it is appropriate only where some inaccuracy is acceptable.
exception: use only when some variation from the accurate result is acceptable for the use case

statement: In a distributed multi-node cache an algorithm keeps values consistent across nodes, but updating many or geographically distributed nodes takes time, during which different nodes hold different values, so the result returned depends on which node serves the request until eventual consistency is reached.

When website content is cached at edge locations worldwide, an update can take a long time to reach every edge, so for a period after a change some users in some regions still receive the old content until all caches are updated; the severity of this depends on the application and is handled with application-specific strategies.

All major cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, IBM Cloud) offer managed open-source Redis, often caching-configured, in many sizes and regions as single instances or with load-balanced read replicas; they are easy to set up, quick to turn on/off, and billed hourly or by resources consumed, making them well-suited to development, testing, and autoscaled production.

Redis Enterprise Cloud is a fully managed DBaaS offering transparent high availability, Active-Active Geo-Distribution, and hybrid/multicloud deployments, available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud (e.g., as the first-party Azure Cache for Redis Enterprise), with a free tier for development and test use.

Managed Redis offerings come with preconfigured standard cloud security, but if you self-host Redis on your own cloud compute instances you are responsible for ensuring the security settings are correct, certificates are valid, and security is maintained.
condition: self-hosting Redis rather than using a managed offering

statement: An open-source Redis deployment consists of one primary plus one or more read replicas; in the cloud the replicas are typically placed in separate availability zones for availability, or in different regions for better geographic read performance, and in principle even across different cloud providers (subject to the provider permitting the replication-setup commands).

Open-source Redis is limited to a single master with read replicas, so all writes must go to that one master; in a multi-region or multicloud deployment only read performance improves via local replicas, while writes must travel back to the single master, significantly hurting write performance.

To improve both read and write performance across regions or clouds you must use a multi-master (Active-Active) topology rather than master-replica; this requires multi-master capability not available in open-source Redis but provided by Redis Enterprise, after which any regional master can serve reads and writes and writes auto-replicate to the other masters.
condition: multi-region or multicloud deployment needing write performance

statement: No major cloud provider offers multi-region Active-Active or cross-provider Redis deployments natively, so achieving that large-scale, highly available distributed architecture requires Redis Enterprise (via Redis Enterprise Cloud or self-hosted instances).

A cache is useful only if it is effective, and what counts as effective depends on the reason for caching — most commonly reducing the number of long or expensive operations to increase the speed and efficiency of request processing.

Cache overhead is the extra time spent interacting with the cache; in a cache-aside strategy it is the cache-check time plus the cache-write time, so a cache miss costs the cache-check + service-call + cache-write (more than calling the service directly) while a cache hit costs only the cache-check (much faster).

A cache is effective only when the total time over all requests is less than it would be without the cache, which essentially requires more cache hits than misses; effectiveness increases both with a higher hit-to-miss ratio and with a larger ratio of service-call time to cache overhead.

A cache becomes more efficient than no cache once its hit rate exceeds a break-even threshold determined by the cache overhead relative to the service call time (for a 25ms service with 2ms overhead, the break-even hit rate is about 7.7%).

The higher the cache hit rate, the more effective the cache: average request time drops dramatically as the hit rate rises (in the worked example, raising the hit rate from 25% to 90% cut average request time from 20.5ms to 3.6ms, about 86% lower than with no cache).

The greater the cost of calling the un-cached service, the greater the cache's effectiveness at a given hit rate (for a 500ms service, a 90% hit rate yields roughly an 89.8% improvement in average request time).

The cache-effectiveness calculation — comparing expected request time with and without the cache given hit rate, overhead, and service call time — can and should be performed for each caching opportunity to determine whether, and to what extent, a cache will help.

Cache locality is the practice of inferring data that will likely be needed from data used in the past and loading it into the cache in advance; it is common in CPU and memory caches, where accessing one memory location often implies nearby locations will be accessed.
Data lag is the time it takes for a value changed on one server to propagate to all other servers in the system.
A cache flush is the action of emptying a cache of all its data, after which subsequent requests result in cache misses until the cache is repopulated.

This book uses cache consistency colloquially to mean whether the cache returns a correct result versus the source, whereas purists distinguish cache coherency: consistency concerns how external requests to a key are ordered so the stored value is correct, while coherency means reads and writes to a key behave as if no cache existed (the same value is returned whether read through the cache or not).
